summary:
The Anti-Homosexuality Act 2023 is in force. It provides the death penalty for "aggravated homosexuality", a category that includes sexual intercourse with a person younger than 18; twenty years' imprisonment for homosexuality or attempted homosexuality; ten years for purporting to contract a same-sex marriage or knowingly attending a purported same-sex marriage ceremony; and three years for a minor convicted of homosexuality. A person convicted of homosexuality or attempted homosexuality cannot be employed in a childcare facility even after release. A provision of the 2023 bill that would have criminalised identifying as gay or non-binary with ten years' imprisonment was proposed but ultimately excluded from the Act.

On 4 April 2024 Uganda's Constitutional Court upheld the Act's core provisions, including the death penalty in certain circumstances and penalties of up to 20 years, rejecting public-participation challenges; the same court had voided a similar 2013 law on procedural grounds.

Same-sex marriage has been constitutionally prohibited since 29 September 2005, when President Museveni signed a constitutional amendment stating "Marriage between persons of the same sex is prohibited."

Enforcement and abuse since the Act: Human Rights Watch's 26 May 2025 report "They're Putting Our Lives at Risk" documents arrests, shelter raids, evictions and public outings unleashed by the Act, with many LGBT people in hiding. In February 2026, Ugandan police arrested two women in Arua after neighbours reported them for allegedly kissing in public, one of the first known arrests under the 2023 Act. In June 2021, a raid on the Happy Family Youth Shelter in Kampala resulted in forty-four arrests, with police claiming an illegal same-sex wedding was being held; several detainees alleged police performed invasive anal examinations. In January 2024 a transgender woman in Kampala was mobbed and beaten into a two-week coma after a false TikTok allegation, sheltering with 20 others at a Kampala safe house. A Reuters report of June 2024 described rights violations against Uganda's LGBTQ community as escalating, according to a pressure group.

Document and identity recognition: in October 2021, trans woman Cleopatra Kambugu Kentaro was issued identification documents identifying her as female, the first Ugandan to have a change of gender legally recognised. The source does not address broader document or legal gender recognition processes beyond this case.

Digital exposure: Access Now (15 May 2025) reports that digital entrapment via dating and social apps is one of the main tactics authorities use against LGBTQ+ people in Uganda, and that the companies behind popular apps do too little to protect users. Amnesty International's 23 October 2024 report "Everybody Here Is Having Two Lives or Names" documents widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence including doxxing, impersonation, hacking and disinformation, and finds the AHA 2023 has fostered a climate of impunity forcing people and organisations to alter how they present themselves online.

The US State Department's travel advisory for Uganda includes LGBT-specific warnings under its 'Do Not Travel' advisory (the page was not retrievable at research time, HTTP 403).

Historical pattern of targeting: in October 2010 the tabloid Rolling Stone published names, addresses, photographs and hangouts of 100 allegedly gay and lesbian Ugandans with a call for their execution; activist David Kato was murdered in 2011 shortly after winning a lawsuit against the paper. Pride Uganda was cancelled in August 2017 after threats of arrest, and in June 2012 the government banned 38 NGOs accused of promoting homosexuality. LGBTQ people in Uganda face severe discrimination actively incited by conservative political, religious and community leaders, with violent attacks and harassment often performed or incited by state officials. The most recent documented killing in this record is from 2011; no later instance is documented here.
tangentialFactors:
The US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report for Uganda listed violence and discrimination against marginalized groups, including the LGBT community, among the three most important human rights problems in the country, dating to the era of the Anti-Homosexuality Bill debates.

Public opinion measures are dated: a 2013 Pew survey found 96 percent of Ugandans believed homosexuality should not be accepted by society, while a 2017 ILGA poll showed 59 percent agreed gay, lesbian and bisexual people should enjoy the same rights as straight people.

Human Rights Watch reported in 2005 that Uganda's abstinence-until-marriage programs discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation, denying young LGBTQ people information that could save their lives and reinforcing stigma. A 2018 article in African Health Sciences stated that Uganda's high HIV rate has roots in stigma against same-sex sexual behaviour and sex work; the source does not address healthcare access barriers specifically for trans people.

Legal gender recognition has been granted in at least one case: in October 2021 trans woman Cleopatra Kambugu Kentaro received identification documents identifying her as female, the first Ugandan to have a change of gender legally recognised. No general legal process for gender recognition is documented in this record.

Amnesty International's October 2024 report finds the AHA 2023 has fostered a climate of impunity forcing LGBTQ Ugandans and organisations to alter how they present themselves online, alongside widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence including doxxing, impersonation, hacking and disinformation.

In June 2012 the government banned 38 NGOs accused of promoting homosexuality. Pride Uganda was cancelled in August 2017 after threats of arrest.
outOfScopeNotes:
The US State Department travel advisory page for Uganda was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the claim that it includes LGBT-specific warnings under the 'Do Not Travel' advisory is carried from secondary description and is unresolved against the primary source.

No general legal process for gender recognition beyond the single 2021 case is documented in this record; whether a statutory mechanism exists is unresolved.

Whether the anal examination allegations from the June 2021 Happy Family Youth Shelter raid were investigated or resulted in any finding is not sourced here.

The Reuters June 2024 claim of escalating violations is attributed to a pressure group's reporting; no independent quantification accompanies it in this inventory.

Trans-specific killing or violence rates against a general homicide baseline are not available in this inventory, so no comparative magnitude can be stated.
